findings.title: Google credential key is overwritten with the zod SafeParse wrapper object
findings.body: `parseRefreshTokenResponse()` returns the result of `schema.safeParse(...)` (i.e. `{ success: true, data: {...} }`), not the parsed object, but the return value is assigned to `key` and written straight into `prisma.credential.update({ data: { key } })`. Previously the code used `googleCredentialSchema.parse(googleCredentials)` which returned the credential object itself. As a result, after the first token refresh the stored Google Calendar credential becomes `{"success":true,"data":{...}}`, which no longer satisfies `googleCredentialSchema` on the next load, permanently breaking Google Calendar for that user. It should store `...data` (and ideally only after checking `success`).

findings.title: minimumTokenResponseSchema computed keys are nonsense and strip every token field except access_token
findings.body: `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]` both evaluate to the string `"[object Object]"` (Zod types have no `toString` override), so the object literal ends up with a single extra key literally named `"[object Object]"`, with the second definition overwriting the first. The resulting schema is effectively `{ access_token: string, "[object Object]": unknown }`. Because `z.object` strips unknown keys by default, when credential sharing is enabled the parsed data loses `expires_in`/`expiry_date`/`refresh_token`/`scope`/etc. Callers that spread `tokenResponse.data` into the stored credential (e.g. office365calendar) will therefore persist a credential with no expiry and a bogus refresh token. The intent ("allow any extra properties, require access_token plus a numeric expiry") needs `.passthrough()` / `z.record()`, not computed keys.

findings.title: Missing refresh_token is replaced with the literal string "refresh_token", destroying valid stored refresh tokens
findings.body: When the provider response has no `refresh_token`, the function sets `refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token = "refresh_token"`. This runs on the normal (non credential-sharing) path too. For providers whose schema makes `refresh_token` optional — e.g. `packages/app-store/office365calendar/lib/CalendarService.ts`, where the result is spread with `{ ...o365AuthCredentials, ...tokenResponse.data }` and persisted — the real, still-valid refresh token in the DB is overwritten with the useless string `"refresh_token"`, so the next refresh fails and the user must reconnect. Only inject a placeholder when it is actually needed, or leave the field absent so the spread keeps the existing token.

findings.title: Credential-sync path returns a fetch Response where callers expect an axios/SDK/gaxios response
findings.body: When credential sharing is enabled the helper returns a raw `fetch` `Response`, but the call sites consume very different shapes: `zoho-bigin` and `zohocrm` read `tokenInfo.data.error` / `tokenInfo.data.access_token` (axios response), `hubspot` assigns the return value to a `HubspotToken` and reads `expiresIn`/`accessToken` (SDK object), and `googlecalendar` reads `res?.data` (gaxios response). A `Response` has none of these properties, so with `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` configured these refresh paths throw `TypeError` or silently store `undefined` tokens. The helper needs to normalise the sync response per call site (or each call site must handle both shapes).

findings.title: `prisma` is used but never imported in Salesforce CalendarService
findings.body: `await prisma.credential.update(...)` was added to `getClient`, but there is no `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma"` in the file (the import list only adds `zod` and `parseRefreshTokenResponse`). This is a compile error under type-check and a `ReferenceError: prisma is not defined` at runtime, which means every Salesforce CalendarService instantiation (i.e. every booking/availability call involving Salesforce) will throw.

findings.title: Salesforce connection is built with the stale access token after refreshing
findings.body: `getClient` fetches a new access token and stores it in the DB, but then constructs `new jsforce.Connection({ ..., accessToken: credentialKey.access_token })` using the *old* token from the credential instead of `accessTokenParsed.data.access_token` (and `instanceUrl: credentialKey.instance_url` instead of the refreshed `instance_url`). The refresh is therefore pointless: all subsequent API calls still use the expired token and will fail with 401/INVALID_SESSION_ID.

findings.title: Salesforce refreshes the token and writes the credential on every service instantiation
findings.body: The new refresh_token request and `prisma.credential.update` run unconditionally inside `getClient`, which is called from the constructor. There is no expiry check (unlike every other app, which only refreshes when the stored token is expired). Every Salesforce CalendarService creation — including availability lookups — now issues a token request to `login.salesforce.com` plus a DB write, which wastes requests, risks hitting Salesforce's OAuth rate limits, and adds latency to the booking path. Gate the refresh on the stored expiry.

findings.title: Refresh success is checked via `response.statusText !== "OK"`
findings.body: `statusText` is not guaranteed to be populated (HTTP/2 and several fetch implementations return an empty string for a 200 response), so this check can throw `HttpError` with an empty message on a perfectly successful token refresh, and it also treats any non-200 2xx as success. Use `response.ok` / `response.status` instead.

findings.title: zoho-bigin passes credentialId where refreshOAuthTokens expects userId
findings.body: `refreshOAuthTokens(fn, "zoho-bigin", credentialId)` — the third parameter of `refreshOAuthTokens` is the Cal.com `userId`, which is sent to the external sync endpoint as `calcomUserId`. Passing the credential's id means that, with credential sharing enabled, the self-hosted endpoint is queried for the wrong user, so either the request fails or (worse) another user's tokens are fetched and stored on this credential. `refreshAccessToken` should receive and forward `credential.userId`.

findings.title: Zoom sends appSlug "zoomvideo" while the app's slug is "zoom"
findings.body: `refreshOAuthTokens(..., "zoomvideo", credential.userId)` sends `appSlug=zoomvideo` to the credential sync endpoint, but the Zoom app's slug everywhere else in the codebase (and in the `App` table / the new `/api/webhook/app-credential` lookup) is `zoom` — see `zoomvideo/api/callback.ts` which creates the credential with `appId: "zoom"`. The self-hoster therefore receives an identifier that does not match the slug it must post back, so Zoom credential syncing cannot work without a special case.

findings.title: Credential sync request carries no authentication and its status is never checked
findings.body: The POST to `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` sends only `calcomUserId` and `appSlug` with no shared secret/signature (contrast with the inbound webhook, which requires `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET`). The remote endpoint therefore cannot distinguish a request from Cal.com from any other caller, so an endpoint implemented as documented hands out user access tokens to anyone who can reach it. The response status is also never checked, so an error page/HTML body is passed on to the caller as if it were a token response. A signed header (or reuse of `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET`) and an `response.ok` check are needed, and the expected request/response contract should be documented.

findings.title: Unvalidated request body and decryption failures produce unhandled 500s; no HTTP method guard
findings.body: `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body)` throws a `ZodError` on a malformed payload, and `symmetricDecrypt(...)` / `JSON.parse(...)` throw on a bad key or non-JSON plaintext. None of these are caught, so the handler returns an unhandled 500 (with a stack trace in the logs/response depending on config) instead of a 400 with a useful message. There is also no method check, so a `GET`/`DELETE` to this route reaches the body parse and 500s. Use `safeParse` + explicit 400s and restrict the handler to POST.

findings.title: Synced credential update does not clear the `invalid` flag
findings.body: When a credential already exists the handler only updates `key`. Credentials that were previously marked `invalid: true` (e.g. by `invalidateCredential` in the Zoom/Webex adapters, or the `invalid_grant` path in Google Calendar) stay flagged after fresh working keys are pushed in, so Cal.com keeps treating the app as broken and shows the "reconnect" state even though the parent application has supplied valid tokens. The update should also set `invalid: false`.

findings.title: Webhook secret compared with `!==` (non constant-time) and header lookup is case-sensitive
findings.body: The shared secret check uses a plain string comparison, which is vulnerable to timing analysis; use `crypto.timingSafeEqual` on equal-length buffers. Additionally, `req.headers[process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME]` relies on the operator configuring a lowercase header name (Node lowercases incoming header keys); if they configure `Calcom-Webhook-Secret` every request silently 403s. Lowercase the configured name before the lookup instead of only documenting the requirement in `.env.example`.

findings.title: No tests for the new credential-sync webhook or token parsing helper
findings.body: This PR adds a new unauthenticated-by-default HTTP surface that writes OAuth credentials into the database (`/api/webhook/app-credential`) plus two shared helpers (`parseRefreshTokenResponse`, `refreshOAuthTokens`) that are now on the refresh path of ~10 apps, and ships with no unit/integration tests (the PR description confirms this). Given that the helpers change the stored credential shape for Google, Office365, Salesforce and others, regressions here silently break every user's calendar/video integrations. At minimum, tests covering secret rejection, create vs update behaviour, and the enabled/disabled branches of the two helpers should be added.
